I'm picky. Very few games are able to hold my attention for more than a few hours, maybe a week of light play. The only games that have ever held my attention as long as PZ are Skyrim, Enderal, and Stardew Valley. Project Zomboid, in my book, is one of the top 20 games of all time. Unique, challenging, and almost infinitely customizable with custom sandbox and a great modding community. The elements I wished were in the game when I started playing continue to be added, or are on the roadmap for the most part, or are covered by mods. I do very much wish for settlers in the style of Fallout 4 settlers, where trading, an in game currency (equivalent to caps in fallout), etc would be added for a more long term play mode, as well as the ability to not just restore utilities (like restore utilities mods), but to fix and reuse the infrastructure on the map and assign settlers to operate them (gasoline production plant, steel manufacturing, mining, etc). But for the things I wish it had, it has many many other things you can do that make you forget you wished for additional features. My hats off to the developers and the modders for creating one of the best games ever.

Project Zomboid: An Important Study Into Why Humans Should Not Be Trusted With Houses

AI DISCLAIMER: No Artificial Intelligence was used in the creation of this review. Any suspiciously elaborate vocabulary, unnecessary philosophical analysis, or perfectly structured paragraphs are entirely the result of natural human intelligence.

Project Zomboid is, at its core, a video game about survival.

But describing it merely as a survival game would be intellectually irresponsible.

Project Zomboid is an interactive investigation into mortality, resource management, architecture, nutrition, carpentry, emotional resilience and the increasingly urgent question of why I am still alive after making that decision.

The game begins with an extremely reasonable premise:

You are going to die.

This is communicated with an admirable level of honesty.

Most games tell you that you are the hero.

Project Zomboid looks you directly in the eyes and says:

“No.”

You are not special.

You are not chosen.

You are not the protagonist of destiny.

You are simply a person who has found a frying pan and is now expected to survive the collapse of civilization.

The gameplay is remarkably detailed.

You must eat.

You must drink.

You must sleep.

You must manage injuries.

You must maintain your clothing.

You must understand your surroundings.

You must avoid zombies.

You must also somehow remember that you left the oven on approximately six hours ago.

This level of realism is extraordinary.

The inventory system is particularly impressive.

You can carry an almost unreasonable number of objects, provided you are willing to destroy your spine in the process.

A hammer becomes valuable.

A screwdriver becomes valuable.

A can opener becomes extremely valuable.

Suddenly, a completely ordinary kitchen becomes a treasure vault.

You enter a house and think:

“Nothing here is useful.”

Ten minutes later:

“I HAVE FOUND TWO CANS OF BEANS.”

Civilization has meaning again.

The zombies are also fascinating.

They are slow.

They are persistent.

They are everywhere.

And, most importantly, they have absolutely no respect for personal boundaries.

You can spend hours preparing the perfect safehouse, reinforcing doors, organizing supplies and creating an elaborate agricultural system.

Then you forget to close one window.

Civilization ends again.

The building mechanics deserve recognition as well.

Project Zomboid allows you to construct and improve your environment, providing a genuine sense of progression.

You begin as a terrified individual hiding inside somebody else's house.

Eventually, you become a carpenter.

Then a farmer.

Then an electrician.

Then a professional collector of approximately 38 different types of canned food.

At some point, you look around your fortified base and realize:

I have successfully recreated society, but I still cannot find a can opener.

This is progress.

The game also understands the importance of psychological consequences.

Your character can become stressed.

Your character can become depressed.

Your character can become anxious.

Honestly, relatable.

The game is essentially capable of simulating the human experience so accurately that I occasionally stop playing and wonder whether Project Zomboid is actually just real life with worse graphics.

The difficulty is brutal, but this is part of its charm.

Every death feels meaningful.

Every mistake teaches you something.

Every successful escape creates confidence.

And every subsequent mistake reminds you that confidence was premature.

This creates a beautiful gameplay cycle.

Hope.

Confidence.

Panic.

Blood.

Loading screen.

A perfect representation of the human condition.

In conclusion, Project Zomboid is an extraordinary survival experience that successfully combines realism, strategy, exploration, resource management and the deeply important activity of staring at a refrigerator for several minutes while deciding whether one yoghurt is worth risking your life for.

I started this game at build 41. It's incredible fun for any RPG fan, who also likes basebuilding games. Getting my initial home secured, building up supplies and learning skills was just the beginning, and that already took many hours of playing. Every item is a win, there is 0 cheesing and you have to scrap for every freaking inch of space. 

Even though the graphics are simple, don't be fooled, this game is VERY deep in it's logic and mechanics. Most things that would frustrate people in zombie/survival games (why can't I do this) is thought off, you can pick up and use the most random stuff, in many ways I never even thought off. 

It's not even a very steep learning curve to get average and survive, but it definitely takes many hours to become good, which is how I like it. I play only single-player, so I couldn't tell you about the community, but from the quality of the game and youtube content out there, I feel like this is growing into an Indie-hit monster more and more every year and deservedly so.

Great game, but very rough around the edges. It isn't for everyone, you need to be able to enjoy open-ended survival/sandbox gameplay for it to click. Reminiscent of some 00s flash/java browser games but turned up to 100. However once you solve survival on a map, and have food, power, rainwater collection, weapons and some other things, the connective tissue between the game's mechanics starts to feel a little bit too loose. I stared down the barrel of a grind where I would risk my entire playtime via permadeath, in order to sneak around the city disassembling TV remotes for small amounts of EXP. A grind is no issue, but grinds upon grinds in order to make basic progress after you already did the hard legwork of getting a functioning/safe base up and running is annoying. The game keeps giving you problems after this point, but too many have known, repetitive solutions that restore the status quo rather than creating new situations

My advice, play on characters you don't intend to live with for about 10-20 hours, experience all of the individual mechanics and then just go into Custom Sandbox and make your own version of the game (or even use mods) cause this is what 90% of players seemingly do, which is a pretty damning verdict to the core base game. The game also struggles with distinction between difficulty and meaningless friction sometimes. Menu navigation is awkward and a little archaic. Base building is annoying because your guy half dies because he has to move a bookcase 4 meters (yes, carrying heavy weights drains HP, who thought of this I've no idea). You end up having 4 bags equipped at once because your guy cannot carry much at all, and yet training Fitness and Strength to remedy this is a Sisyphean grind equivalent to an Old School Runescape skill once it hits level 94 so there isn't really an easy way around this. This is just one example of many where you can tell what the intent is, but whether it produces a fun outcome, or even an emergent story is another. Much of the game's labour after a certain point becomes busy-work maintenance loops that sometimes struggle to increase player agency, and do not reliably reinforce themselves or supply the player with reasons to continue engaging with the world which is a shame. More random events like the Helicopter, survivor NPC AIs or even loose world-factions/bandits could go some way to offset this. I half expected to wake up in my base to have found zombies had discovered the sound of my generator running outside and I'd have to fight off a horde in order to survive. It never happened. The only times I felt at risk of dying were when I made stupid decisions, and yet if you play in a logical way, avoiding risk, it becomes strangely boring which is a kind of strange, negative feedback loop.

"This is how you died" is cool, until you actually survive and realise the game's best moments are in the first third of a character's life and the latter two thirds are inventory management, reading books whilst in 3x speed, grocery runs, water runs and occasionally mending your generator. The premise for failure is exciting which is great, but the premise for success is often lacking. Other sandbox games encourage interaction with the world in much more meaningful ways even if they too have permadeath mechanics.

I also feel like it suffers from the same thing that a lot of indie games do, where development priorities are incohesive and ignore core functional issues in order to tinker at the edges, tending to build the game wide rather than tall. Raising animals is a great idea and one I definitely would've added, but when base building itself is so buggy and annoying, maybe fix that first. Similar to other indie simulation games, it sometimes feels like a skyscaper built on sand. A game doesn't need 4 different kinds of can opener when moving a crate or dragging a corpse leaves your guy basically needing a hospital bed to recover

That said, the core of the game does have soul, and there is an amazing amount of potential here if you can stomach the wait between various builds of the game. I enjoyed my time spent and it's probably worth the price it's sold at, despite having issues. It is a topaz in the rough that could become a diamond but might need a lot of buffering and a little bit of Alchemy to get there.

I'm conflicted with this game. It's brilliant, yet at the same time frustrating. Imagine 7D2D had a threesome with The Sims and The Walking Dead and you get Project Zomboid.

It's probably the deepest, most realistic zombie survival game there is. The level of detail is insane - right down to turning an oven on, setting it's temperature and waiting for the food to cook. Or replacing very specific parts on a car - such as break disks. Leave your lights on and it'll drain the 12V battery. It's almost an*l levels of detail. If you love that sort of thing, this game will appeal to you. 

However, the extreme realism is also it's downfall. Realism is great in games, but it needs to be balanced with fun. I feel PZ goes too heavy on the realism and ends up being grindy and painfully slow. An in-game year takes around 876 hours in real-time, which is nuts. Sure you'll fast forward a fair chunk of that, but given it take months to actually grow crops, I expect a lot of players won't even get through the first in-game month. And then there's learning skills - be prepared to be bored to tears trying to learn skills, even with the book multipliers active it's slow AF. PZ could also be described as an inventory management simulator, there's millions of items and combinations.

The control system is awkward too, and very poorly explained. Furthermore, killing zombies seems to be a side quest rather than the main focus.

But despite this, the game is actually really good. It plays well, when you get the hang of it and it's crazy addictive with an insane amount of things to do (far too many IMO). I feel a lot of issues in this game would be mitigated by playing with friends, but I'm a loner and don't have any(!)

Great game. Still playing after rage quitting about 10 times in the first 30 hours. There is zero handholding and can be extremely unforgiving at times. The game is a slowburn over what could take months. Which is good. Too many games are over in 100 hours and you miss out on a lot of content that way. The game needs someone with self motivation. There is zero purpose other than survive.

Points of fun
Combat
Cars
Exploring
Foraging
Movement
Environmental interactions
Cooking
Teamwork in multiplayer

Points of rage
Crafting. This makes the whole game rage inducing. It feels like it was made by 15 different people with 20 different ideas each on how it should be done and no one told them no. Everything runs on what feels like a different system and you have to figure out how each system works and none of it is cohesive. The whole thing is a mess. Please just pick a menu system and stick to it. 

Building. This has the same criticism as crafting. 

Repairing Gear. The system to repair is to click the thing that repairs the item instead of the item you want repaired. Meanwhile for things like cooking, you click the thing you want to add things to instead of the thing you want to add. It's all very confusing.

Books. I do not love that if the character dies you have to re-read every single book for an xp boost to a skill. A Book takes forever to read. A 5 to 10 minute AFK system in game is not riveting game play. Makes books in multiplayer where you cannot speed up time a very annoying time sink. Then you get to do it all over again.

Game is fun. Still playing. Blood pressure still going up.

Hate yourself? Like suffering? Playing this because a friend bet you wouldn't? Reading the reviews 'cause why not? Play Project Zomboid. Those goofy little pricks are going to make your day (not) wonderful.

For people who like reading:
I could go on and write an essay on this game, so I'll chop it down to the basics.
This is a great survival game, better than 7DTD I must say. Will I get bored of this game? Short answer, no. With friends or not, mods or not, you will have a great time. Solves any issue involving being bored. The zomboids... We speak nothing but pure comedy with Rosewood and that one KSP car, too many zomboids blocking out the Rosewood bookstore? KSP. Want the guns in the RPD? KSP. Want to level up carpentry? KSP. Solve all your problems with a police car.
The fun part is abusing the zomboids, however that ranging from running them over (be a mechanic lol) to target practice (With silencer if you don't have much ammo). Are they annoying? Yes. Will they give you a heart attack? Absolutely. Zomboid population at max? Good luck, you might not even get out of the house without dying. Cars? I hear the weewoos coming back to me.

for lazy people: Play the game, it's fun.
